extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in Korean literature
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of Korean literary history, major poetic and prose forms, oral traditions, and modern developments from ancient times through the twentieth century. Describes formal features, typical themes, and historical/contextual influences for each form or period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosodic basis of Korean poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: The basis of Korean prosody is a line of alternating groups of three or four syllables, which is probably the most natural rhythm to the language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Korean poetry originally was meant to be sung; forms and styles reflect melodic origins and this alternating 3-4 syllable grouping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyangga formal rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyangga poems may consist of four, eight or ten lines; ten-line poems are structured into three sections with four, four, and two lines respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many ten-line hyangga were written by Buddhist monks; themes often include Buddhist topics and death; only 25 survive (Samguk yusa contains 14, Gyunyeojeon 11).

rubrics_metrics.name: Idu / hyangchal writing method
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyangga were written in Korean using modified hanja in a system called idu; the variety used for hyangga was sometimes called 'hyangchal'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Idu uses hanja characters partly for meaning and partly for pronunciation, so some characters consistently stand for Korean words; the system may appear complicated but becomes consistent with use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goryeo songs (byeolgok/changga) characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Goryeo songs are characterized by a refrain in the middle or at the end of each stanza, lack of clear form, increased length, and frank, powerful language often about love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They were transmitted orally, often sung with musical accompaniment by kisaeng; two distinct forms exist—dallyeonche (single-stanza shorter form) and yeonjanche (extended multi-stanza form).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sijo structural rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Sijo are characterized by a structure of three stanzas of four feet each; each foot contains three to four syllables except on the third stanza where the 1st foot is supposed to have 3 syllables and the 2nd foot can have as many as seven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sijo became popular in the Joseon period and often reflect Confucian thought (themes like loyalty); they were popular with common people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gasa form and thematic scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Gasa is a form of verse with twinned feet of three or four syllables each; its content can include moral admonitions and may be regarded by some as a form of essay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common themes include nature, the virtues of gentlemen, or love between man and woman; gasa is a simple verse form capable of extended didactic content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goryeo/Byeolgok refrain usage
rubrics_metrics.description: A defining characteristic of Goryeo songs is the presence of a refrain either in the middle or at the end of each stanza which establishes mood or links disparate parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The refrain carries the melody and spirit of the poem and can unify poems composed of discrete parts with differing contents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prose divisions and sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Korean prose literature can be divided into narratives, fiction, and literary miscellany; principal narrative sources include Samguk sagi and Samguk yusa compiled in Classical Chinese.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narratives include myths, legends, and folktales; Samguk yusa also contains Buddhist saint lives and hyangga; Koryo-era compilations preserved prehistoric and early historical stories used later as sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiction classification by language, length, and social perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Fiction is classified by language (written in Chinese vs Korean), by length (short one-chapter, 'medium' ~10 chapters, long >10 chapters), and by author social class (yangban vs commoner).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works are usually didactic with happy endings; yangban-authored fiction tends to be set in China while commoner-authored fiction is set in Korea; many works derived from earlier narratives with added incidents and characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary miscellany topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary miscellany consists of jottings by the yangban on history, biography, autobiography, and poetic criticism, serving as an outlet for personal expression outside official Chinese prose genres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These miscellanies portray customs and manners of their times and are essential for understanding historical social spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pansori-based fiction characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Pansori-based fiction originated from five orally transmitted pansori and is characterized by human stereotypes of ordinary people; it was composed in its present form in the 1870s and became widely read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pansori texts were narrative in origin and later expanded into p'ansori fiction; transformation from poetry to narrative was facilitated by the inherently narrative nature of pansori.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral literature categories and performance features
rubrics_metrics.description: Oral literature includes ballads, legends, mask plays, puppet-show texts, and p'ansori texts, categorized by singer, subject matter, and regional style; mask plays and puppet shows often contain satiric social criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mask plays allowed actor improvisation, audience vocal response, no fixed stage limits, and achieve dramatic unity through repetition and variety; puppet plays plotlines expose malfeasance of ruling classes; many oral texts were only recorded after Hangul’s invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: P'ansori textual evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: P'ansori texts were first recorded in the 19th century as verse and later expanded into p'ansori fiction; the original repertoire had 12 madang, of which only five are still sung today.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Texts evolved gradually from legends and were altered as they passed between performers; oral transmission led to expansion and variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yongbi eocheonga cultural and literary significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Yongbi eocheonga (Songs of the Dragons Flying to Heaven) was the first Korean text to depart from reliance on Chinese characters and be recorded in Hangul; it conveys nationalism and cultural independence while reflecting Confucian rejection of Buddhism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compiled under King Sejong by a committee of Confucian philologists and literati, composed in 125 cantos, and used to legitimize the Joseon dynasty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sinchesi (new poetry) and Jayusi (free verse) characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Sinchesi ('new poetry') abandoned the fixed metaphor of classical Korean poetry and was influenced by the French vers libre; it contributed to the formation of modern free verse (jayusi).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This movement developed alongside the modernisation of Korean literature in the late 19th and early 20th centuries and was linked to Hangul's development and increased literacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern literature influences and markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern Korean literature was strongly influenced by Western aesthetic schools, Christianity, and the development/popularity of Hangul, which increased literacy and enabled the rise of professional writers and sinsoseol (novels in Hangul).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First printed Korean fiction example: Pilgrim's Progress translation (1893); modern forms were also propagated by newspapers and magazines emerging after the Gabo Reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature under Japanese rule: 'New Novel' themes and constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: 'New Novel' (circa 1906–c.1917) involved realistic problems—self-reliance, freedom of association, new education, enlightenment, destruction of tradition—and later literature during Japanese rule grappled with censorship and ideological coercion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literary magazines of the 1920s–30s were important for development but many were shut down in the 1940s; writers experimented with styles to address colonial realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-war thematic developments
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-1945 literature (both North and South) developed themes centered on the wounds and chaos of war, daily lives of ordinary people, collapse of traditional values, national division (bundan soseol), and political expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Movements included traditionalist revivals of folk rhythms, experimentalists bringing new experiences to poetry, 1960s writers rejecting sentimental post-war literature and engaging with political reality, and 1970s anti-establishment/industrialization concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation and international reception criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Until the 1980s Korean literature was largely ignored by non-Korean speakers; since then both the diversity of translated books and the quality of translations have improved, aided by institutions like LTI Korea and increased interest due to Korean film.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anthologies (e.g., Flowers of Fire, 1974) were early English-language introductions; film and cultural exports have increased demand for translations.
